en: Annotated Essentials of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty; second translation.
Annotated by the Northern Tianmu Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu.
The main text consists of three parts: first, the homage and statement of intent; second, the formal enumeration of the precepts; third, the conclusion indicating the essential purpose.
The first and third parts were both added by the compilers. The second part, the formal enumeration of the precepts, is derived from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the "Chapter on Ethics" within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the Master Paramārtha had already previously completed a translation of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*.
This present work is now translated anew as a separate recension; therefore, it is designated as the second translation.
The first part has four sections: 1. Taking refuge; 2. Admonishing the listeners; 3. Praising through analogy; 4. Exhorting to uphold. First, taking refuge:
I take refuge in Vairocana, The Vajra Buddhas of the ten directions, And also pay homage to the former masters of this treatise.
One should realize that the Honored One Maitreya is Vairocana;
this is translated as "Pure and Perfect. Because all evils are severed without exception, he is pure; because all virtues are practiced without exception, he is perfect.

He immediately perfected his cultivation of virtue to its ultimate limit and fully realized his original nature, becoming endowed with the three bodies (trikāya) and eternally dwelling in the land of recompense.
He was thus the Great Preceptor of the Bodhisattva Precepts. As for the Vajra Buddha of the ten directions, he is the indestructible nature realized after the Vajra Path;
he is likewise the Perfectly Full Body of Recompense, one in body and one in wisdom with Rocana.
The powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are likewise; each pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, being unobstructed and unmixed, neither identical nor different.

They are the venerable witnesses of the same altar for the Bodhisattva precepts. The Venerable Maitreya—called Mili in Sanskrit—was previously the master of the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) and will subsequently become a Buddha; he is the *karmācārya* for the Bodhisattva precepts.
Ācārya: As I am about to recite the precepts, I first take refuge and pay homage to seek their empowerment.
2. Admonition to Listen:
Now I shall speak the Threefold Aggregate Precepts; may all Bodhisattvas listen together.
These very precepts of heavy and light offenses can sever all evils; this is the morality of restraining oneself (saṃvara-śīla). They can accomplish all virtues;
this is the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla). They can benefit sentient beings; this is the morality of benefiting living beings (sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla).
III. Praise by Way of Simile:
Precepts are like a great bright lamp, capable of dispelling the darkness of the long night.
Precepts are like a true jewel mirror, illuminating all phenomena without omission. Precepts are like a *maṇi* gem, raining down objects to relieve the poor and destitute.

The "Great Bright Lamp" is a metaphorical praise for the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint), which can sever all the darkness of evil karma, ignorance, and delusion throughout the long night of birth and death.

The "True Precious Mirror" is a metaphorical praise for the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts of gathering wholesome dharmas), which can illuminate all the qualities of merit and wisdom of the Buddha-ground.
The "Maṇi Jewel" is a metaphorical praise for the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precepts of benefiting sentient beings); as [it is said]:
The wish-fulfilling jewel can rain down all noble wealth, universally relieving the suffering of poverty throughout the nine realms.
○ Fourth, the exhortation to uphold:
To leave the world and swiftly attain Buddhahood, this Dharma alone is supreme; therefore, all Bodhisattvas [should uphold it].

One should diligently protect and uphold [the Dharma], for it is not by being detached from the world that one can deliver others from it. Just as a person standing on the shore can rescue someone drowning in the water, so too must one remain in the world to save others.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s "Universal Worthy’s Constant Practice" is also titled the "Detachment from the World" chapter; detachment from the world refers to descending to transform sentient beings.

This is my fundamental aspiration; attaining Buddhahood is my long-cherished vow for the supreme pursuit. In seeking the supreme above and transforming those below, these three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*) are paramount.
How could one not diligently protect and uphold them? This concludes the introductory statement of intent following the initial act of taking refuge and paying homage.

II. The Second Part: The Correct Enumeration of the Precept Characteristics. This has two sections: first, the explanation of the four grave offenses; second, the explanation of the forty-one light offenses.
Within the first section (the four grave offenses), there are three parts: first, the general heading; second, the specific enumeration; third, the concluding inquiry. Now, the first part.
O Great Beings, these four *pārājika* dharmas are the *bodhisattva-mātṛkā*, spoken in harmony [with the teachings].
*Pārājika* is translated as "abandoned offense" (*qi-zui*), because one who commits this offense is forever abandoned outside the ocean of the Buddha's Dharma.

It is also translated as "extreme evil," because it directly contravenes the supreme and wondrous wholesome dharmas. Furthermore, it is translated as "falling offense," because one falls into the three miserable realms (*trāya*) to undergo [suffering].
Because it is suffering. Furthermore, it is the opposite of grave offenses; because its transgressions are so deep and heavy, they are not easily repented or eliminated.

*Mātṛkā* (摩得勒伽) means "Mother of Wisdom" (*jñānamātṛkā*), as it skillfully explains the characteristics and meanings of all phenomena and is able to give rise to wisdom; this refers specifically to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding those who speak in harmony: only when they dwell in the same location without mutual conflict or contention can they act in accordance with the Dharma.
[This concerns] the recitation of the precepts. Question: The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* fully elucidates ten grave offenses; why does this [text], translated from the Hu language, list only four? Answer:
The Bodhisattva precept-dharma applies universally to all seven classes of practitioners. If one is an upāsaka or upāsikā, they must have already previously received the five precepts.
If one is a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, they must have already previously received the ten precepts. As for a śikṣamāṇā...
One must have already previously received the six dharmas. Whether it be a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, one must have already previously received full ordination (*upasampadā*);

there is absolutely no principle for receiving these bodhisattva precepts alone. Therefore, the four fundamental precepts common to all paths have already been clarified within the precepts of the seven classes of followers;
they will not be repeated here. Now, we shall simply clarify the superior bodhisattva precepts.

Furthermore, regarding these four precepts, it is permitted to receive them again if they are lost; however, for those who have committed the offenses of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying, one must perceive auspicious signs [of purification]. Therefore, they are not listed here together with the others.

Moreover, while a Bodhisattva may, for the sake of sentient beings, permit the transgression of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—as extensively clarified in the Tang translation—the present four grave offenses are strictly prohibited and never permitted; thus, they alone are listed separately.
II. The four individual categories are as follows: first, the precept against praising oneself and disparaging others; second, the precept against stinginess regarding wealth and the Dharma;
third, the precept against being angry and refusing to accept repentance; fourth, the precept against slandering and disturbing the true Dharma.
△ First, the precept against praising oneself and disparaging others:
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of craving gain, praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is called the first *pārājika* offense.
To praise one's own virtues is to extol one's own merits in order to highlight the faults of others; to disparage others is to borrow their shortcomings to manifest one's own excellence.
By thus comparing oneself with others, one seeks to ensure that all gain and offerings accrue solely to oneself.

This directly violates the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), and therefore constitutes a grave offense. If one praises oneself out of greed without disparaging others, or [if one does so] out of anger...
To disparage others while not praising oneself is subsumed under the subsequent section on the transgression of disregarding the precepts.
△ Second, the precept against being stingy with wealth and the Dharma:
If a bodhisattva possesses personal wealth but, due to a nature of stinginess, does not provide for destitute and suffering sentient beings who have come to him for refuge;
To fail to give to those who seek, out of a lack of compassion; or to be stingy and refuse to teach the Dharma to those who wish to hear it—this is called the second *pārājika* offense.

The path of a bodhisattva should always embrace sentient beings through the two gifts of material wealth and the Dharma. By possessing one's own wealth, it is shown that there is no lack of resources.
By [helping] sentient beings who are poor and suffering, it is shown that they do not seek beyond what is reasonable or act with improper greed.

By [teaching] those who wish to hear the Dharma, it is shown that they are not incapable of hearing it. By not withholding the teaching out of stinginess, it is shown that one is not ignorant of the Dharma.
Furthermore, to be stingy, miserly, and narrow-minded, failing to give rise to a heart of compassion, directly contravenes the path to Great Bodhi; therefore, this too constitutes a grave offense.
△ Third, the precept against anger and refusing repentance:
If a bodhisattva, out of malice, utters coarse and evil words, yet their intent does not cease, and they further strike with their hand or inflict blows with a staff.
Like a stone, he is cruel and terrifying; his hatred is predominant. When an offender seeks repentance, he does not accept the confession;
harboring resentment, he does not relinquish it. This is called the third *pārājika* offense.
A single thought of anger already violates the path of gathering in sentient beings; how much more so when one utters evil words with the mouth or inflicts blows with the body?
When one adds evil through both body and speech, one has already lost the mind of compassion;
how much more so when one rejects and refuses to accept repentance? By abandoning sentient beings, one thus loses the Dharma of a Bodhisattva.
△ Fourth: The Precept Against Slandering and Distorting the True Dharma.

If a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, teaches counterfeit dharmas, and zealously establishes counterfeit dharmas—whether understanding them through his own mind or receiving them from another—this is called the fourth *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "similar dharmas": these are not actually the true Dharma, yet they resemble the true Dharma.
It is like purple dye overpowering vermilion, or the music of Zheng disturbing the refined music of Ya. This is precisely what is called slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;

it does not necessarily require verbal abuse or revilement to be termed slander. Furthermore, even if there were such abuse, the offense would still be relatively light, because it cannot delude or confuse people.
To preach a counterfeit Dharma is a transgression even more grave, for it is most capable of misleading and deluding others.

There are generally two types of those who zealously establish such counterfeit Dharmas: first, those who understand it through their own minds, meaning they employ forced interpretation and perverse enlightenment;
second, those who receive it from others, meaning they accept false teachings and stubbornly form factions.
A false teacher. These two cases both contravene the supramundane True Dharma; therefore, they constitute grave offenses. The second section, the detailed enumeration, is concluded.
III. Conclusion and Inquiry:
"O Great Beings, the four *pārājika* dharmas have already been explained. If a bodhisattva, giving rise to superior afflictions, commits one..."
There is one dharma by which one loses the bodhisattva precepts and should receive them again. Now I ask the great beings:
Are you pure in this matter? (Ask three times. The great beings are pure in this matter, for they remain silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld.
"Excessive afflictions" refers to superior-grade greed, or superior-grade stinginess, superior-grade anger, or superior-grade false understanding.
"Committing any one of these offenses" means committing any one of the four dharmas; by doing so, one loses the bodhisattva precepts.
This means that one has lost the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) precept-body (*śīlaskandha*) induced by great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). One should receive it again;

that is, one should profoundly reform previous transgressions and once more arouse the superior mind of great enlightenment (*adhimātra-mahābodhicitta*) as an antidote to superior afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a transgression occurs during the half-month, one must certainly confess and repent after it but before reciting the precepts.

Having already performed repentance, one regains purity; therefore, when it comes time for the formal recitation of the precepts, one remains silent together with those who have not violated the precepts.
This silence serves as the manifestation of purity, and one should always maintain this discipline regarding the precepts in this manner.
Question: Suppose one has previously committed an offense but forgot it and did not repent; only now, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, does one suddenly remember and become aware of it.
Should one immediately go before the assembly to confess, or should one remain silent? If one goes before the assembly to confess, it would be improper to declare that they remain silent;
yet if one remains silent, does this not constitute the offense of concealment (*paticchādana*)? Answer: The Vinaya provides for this.
At that time, even if one personally remembers having committed an offense, one should [confess] toward a fellow practitioner who is of like mind.
One should confess orally and, once the matter has concluded, perform repentance and removal according to the Dharma.
Even if no one with whom to agree can be found, one should form this thought: "Once the matter is finished, I shall confess and remove it before a pure bhikṣu.
Having formed this thought, even if one remains silent while listening, one does not incur the offense of concealment. This concludes the initial explanation of the four pārājika offenses.
II. Explaining the Forty-one Minor Offenses. 1. General Introduction; 2. Detailed Enumeration; 3. Concluding Inquiry. Now, the first:
"O Great Beings, these numerous *duṣkṛta* (minor transgressions) of the Bodhisattva constitute the Bodhisattva-mātṛkā. And so forth.
Taken together,
these are called *duṣkṛta* (translated as "evil-doing"), which refers to impure offenses involving intentional action.
Regarding the phrase "numerous," although forty-one items are listed in the following text, this is because the matters within each individual item are not uniform.

II. A detailed enumeration of the forty-one [precepts]: First, the precept against failing to make offerings to the Triple Gem (up to) the forty-first, the precept against using supernatural powers for neither conversion nor restraint.
△ First, the precept against failing to make offerings to the Triple Gem:
If a bodhisattva abiding in the *vinaya* precepts, for even a single day and night, fails to make offerings to the Buddha—
whether he is present in the world— or to a stūpa or temple, or to the Dharma, or to a scripture, or to the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka, or to the Bodhisattva Mātṛkā...

[The section on] the Treasury. If a bhikṣu-saṃgha, or a multitude of great bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions, are not offered even a small amount of offerings, or even a single prostration;
or if one does not praise the merits of the Triple Gem with even a single verse;
or if one is unable to purify the mind for even a single moment—this is called committing many offenses. Whether due to a lack of respect, or due to indolence, or...
If committed through indolence, this offense arises from defilement. If committed through forgetfulness or error, the offense does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense for a Bodhisattva who has entered the Stage of Pure Mind, who—like a Bhikṣu who has attained unshakable purity—constantly makes offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha according to the established rites.

Abiding in the morality of restraint means that one has received and attained the bodhisattva precepts, and does not violate them, does not abandon them, and is not deranged, distracted, or possessed of a diseased mind.
"The Buddha being present, as well as his stūpas and temples" refers collectively to the Jewel of the Buddha as the object of offering.
"Dharma" refers to what was proclaimed from the Golden Mouth; "scriptures" refers to what was transmitted on palm leaves. The Bodhisattva...
The *Sūtra-piṭaka* specifically refers to the Mahāyāna sūtras; the *Bodhisattva-mātṛkā-piṭaka* specifically refers to the Mahāyāna śāstras and commentaries.
These collectively enumerate the Jewel of the Dharma as the object of veneration.

The community of bhikṣus is the outward manifestation of world-transcendence and the embodiment of the supreme field of merit; it consists of the assembly of great bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

As for these [beings]: the three grades of worthies and the ten stages of sages, whose supernatural powers manifest as shadows and echoes and whose forms have no fixed standard, yet whose resolve is set upon Bodhi—this collectively refers to the Sangha Jewel as the object of offering.
A Bodhisattva abiding in the precepts, regarding the Three Jewels, must perform offerings through the three karmas within each day and night.
Even if the physical karma is minimal, one must at least offer a single prostration; as for the verbal karma...
Even the very least must include a single verse of praise. Even the most minimal mental action must include a single moment of pure mind.
If one cannot even cultivate such a minimal offering, then one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding what is called "numerous offenses," this refers to the numerous *duṣkṛta* dharmas mentioned in the preceding text. Within these numerous offenses:
There are two kinds of discrimination: first, that which arises from defilement—or, conversely, heavy stains—which should be confessed before others;
second, that which does not arise from defilement—or, conversely, light stains—which should be addressed by self-reproach of the mind. As for the Bodhisattva who has entered the Ground of Pure Mind:

according to the General Teaching (Pāṭha-sāmānya), this refers to those from the Ground of Insight (darśana-bhūmi) upward; according to the meaning of connecting the Distinct Teaching (viśeṣa) with the General Teaching, it refers to...

The first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). If considered according to its ultimate meaning, this corresponds to the initial dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*) and the initial faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*).

Having severed the delusions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*), its status is equal to that of the first fruit (*prathamaphala*). Therefore, it is said that he is "like a bhikṣu who has attained indestructible purity (*akṣaya-śuddhi*).
If a bhikṣu realizes the first fruit, he attains indestructible purity regarding the Triple Gem and the precepts; thus, he is said to "constantly make offerings of the true Dharma."
One nurtures the Three Jewels. It should be understood that when a bodhisattva enters the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*), it is likewise so.

Even if one does not perform prostrations or praises with body and speech, the mind never deviates from the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. (Having attained unshakable purity toward the Buddha, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever take refuge in external paths or celestial deities.

Having attained unshakable purity toward the Dharma, even if heterodox teachings were to be intermingled with the True Dharma, one can discern their falsity; and even if the True Dharma were to be mixed with heterodox teachings, one can recognize its correctness. Ultimately, one never relies upon...)

Regarding the scriptures of non-Buddhists, he attains unshakable confidence in the Saṃgha; seeing the ultimate and pure Saṃgha, he reveres and draws near to them; seeing those who are like mute sheep and those who lack shame, he feels compassion and protects them, never giving rise to arrogance or thoughts of falling back.

One shall never rely on the heterodox paths or false assemblies, but attain unshakable purity regarding the precepts; rather than sacrificing one's body or life, one shall never violate the pure precepts received from all Buddhas.
△ Second, the precept against coveting material wealth:
If a bodhisattva has many desires and lacks contentment, and greedily clings to material wealth, this is called a transgression of the many offenses (anekāpatti).

This is a transgression arising from defilement (kliṣṭa-samutthita). There is no offense if, for the sake of severing that [greed], one applies desire and skillful means to adopt the remedies (pratipakṣa). (And there is no offense...)
However, because their natures are sharp, afflictions arise repeatedly;
these are formed through habituation, each having its own predominant tendency, such as a fondness for wealth, beauty, fame, or food.
Once a bodhisattva has understood which of his habitual afflictions from past lives is the most violent and intense, he must certainly sever it.
In order to sever those [afflictions], one must certainly give rise to a wholesome aspiration for the Buddha-dharma, contemplate various skillful means, and embrace them as antidotes.

For example, one who has much greed cultivates the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), while one who has much anger cultivates the meditation on loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*) and so forth.
If one has already diligently applied these remedial means, yet this sharp-natured affliction still repeatedly...
If [the thought] arises, it is simply beyond remedy; one should merely continue to give rise to superior, wholesome aspiration, and thus it shall not be called a transgression of the precepts.
All that is stated in the subsequent text for the purpose of severing those [defilements] follows this same principle.
△ Third, the precept against disrespecting those of equal Dharma:
If a bodhisattva, upon seeing a senior or virtuous person who is a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, out of arrogance or resentment fails to show respect, does not yield his seat,
and does not respond at all to inquiries or requests for the Dharma, this is called committing a multitude of offenses.

If it is committed with a defiled mind, it is an offense arising from defilement. If it is committed through laziness, indolence, a neutral state of mind, or forgetfulness, it is an offense arising from non-defilement.

There is no offense if one is seriously ill, if the mind is distracted, if one is asleep while the others (such as the elders) perceive one to be awake and come to inquire after one's well-being or request the Dharma, or if one truly was asleep and did not respond because of this—these are called cases of no offense. Furthermore, there is no offense if the elder is preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, when engaging in formal debate (*vāda*), whether one is preaching the Dharma oneself, listening to the Dharma, or debating for oneself;
or whether one is in an assembly for preaching the Dharma or in an assembly for formal debate—prostrating at a lower level is not an offense.

This applies if one protects the mind of the speaker, or uses skillful means to subdue them so that they may abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome dharmas, or if one is observing the regulations of the Saṃgha. If...
To protect the minds of many (one does not prostrate or respond; in all such cases, there is no offense).
One who has previously received the precepts is called an *upādhyāya* (senior). One who fully maintains the precepts is called one of virtue.
Those who equally maintain the pure Bodhisattva precepts are called fellow-practitioners (*sahadharma*). These are all persons worthy of respect. "Arrogance" means relying on oneself.
"Arrogance" means to despise others. "Malice and resentment" means to harbor vexation and anger in the mind. "A distracted mind" means to suffer from the affliction of mental derangement.
"When discussing the definitive treatises" means when deliberating upon the true Dharma and Vinaya. The rest may be understood accordingly. Question: Regarding the first precept...
Laziness and indolence arise from defiled fetters; why then do these [present faults] not arise from defiled fetters? Answer:

To abide in the precepts yet fail to make offerings to the Triple Gem is a grave transgression. However, the present failure to respect those of superior, middling, or inferior seats involves only individuals and not yet the Saṃgha as a whole;
therefore, the transgression is somewhat lighter. Nevertheless, even if it does not arise from defilement, if one does not reproach it...
Regretting [the offense] in one's heart removes it; yet this can also obstruct the Bodhisattva precepts. Do not treat even a minor transgression lightly, thinking that it will bring no calamity.
△ Fourth: The Precept Regarding Improper Acceptance of Offerings.
If a Bodhisattva is invited by a donor, whether they go to the donor’s own home, to a monastery, or to another house...
If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of anger or pride, does not accept or go to receive various offerings such as food, clothing, and other requisites, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This offense arises from defilement. There is no offense if one is ill, lacks strength, is insane, is in a remote location, or if there are dangers and difficulties on the road;
or if one knows that by not accepting them, it will lead the donor to discipline themselves, abandon evil, and abide in goodness.
If one has previously accepted an invitation; if one is practicing wholesome dharmas and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment;

if one desires to hear unprecedented teachings on beneficial meanings and definitive treatises; if one knows that the inviter acts out of deceit or malice; if one wishes to protect the feelings of many people who might harbor resentment;
or if one is observing the regulations of the Saṃgha.
To refuse an invitation out of anger or pride directly contravenes the Bodhisattva path of compassionate inclusion;
therefore, this constitutes a grave defiled offense that must be confessed. "Insanity" refers to mental disorders such as derangement and the like.
△ Fifth, the precept against refusing gifts:
If a bodhisattva has a donor offer various precious objects such as gold, silver, pearls, mani-jewels,
and lapis lazuli, and the bodhisattva, out of anger or pride, refuses them in opposition to the donor's intent, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This constitutes an offense arising from defilement, because one has abandoned sentient beings. If it arises from indolence or laziness, it is an offense not arising from defilement.

There is no offense if, upon knowing that after receiving [the gift], the recipient will certainly give rise to craving and attachment; or if, upon knowing that after receiving it, the donor will feel regret; or if, upon knowing that after receiving it, the donor will fall into confusion;
or if, upon knowing that after receiving it, the donor will suffer from poverty and distress; or if one knows that this object is [of such a nature]. It is the third.

It is permitted as a treasure. However, if one knows that an object was obtained through robbery, or if one knows that having accepted it will result in much suffering—namely, being killed, bound, exiled, fined, stripped of wealth, or rebuked—one should not accept it.
"Permitted by the Three Jewels" means that it has already been granted by the Three Jewels; it refers to property belonging to the Three Jewels.
Sixth, regarding the precept against not giving the Dharma:
If a bodhisattva, when sentient beings come to him desiring to hear the Dharma, should harbor anger, resentment, stinginess, or jealousy, [he commits an offense].
To fail to preach the Dharma for someone constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This offense arises from defilement if one fails out of indolence or laziness;

it does not arise from defilement if one fails due to illness or insanity. There is no offense if the person belongs to a non-Buddhist sect seeking to find fault, or if one is gravely ill, or if one is insane.
If one knows that not speaking will bring them to discipline; if the Dharma one practices has not yet been mastered;

if one knows that the person before them is unable to show respect or compliance and their deportment is disordered; or if they are of dull faculties and would give rise to fear upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma.
If one knows that upon hearing it, wrong views will increase; or if one knows that upon hearing it, one will disparage [the teaching] and fall away;
or if, having heard it, one will speak of it to evil people.
Question: How does this differ from the "stinginess regarding the Dharma" among the four pārājika offenses? Answer: That refers to the case of superior-grade afflictions.

This constitutes a grave offense. This is because it pertains to middling or inferior afflictions; therefore, the offense is light. Furthermore, according to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, the offense is classified as grave only if one adds verbal abuse.
In the present case, although there is stinginess and attachment, there is no necessary addition of abuse; therefore, the offense is classified as light.
△ Seventh: The Precept Against Failing to Instruct on the Repentance of Faults.

If a bodhisattva, toward sentient beings who are fierce, evil, and have transgressed the precepts, out of a mind of hatred, either abandons them themselves or prevents others from assisting them, and thus fails to instruct and transform them, this is called a transgression of many offenses. This is a transgression arising from defilement. [If it is due to] laziness...
It is due to indolence or negligence. If one forgets [the rule] and prevents another from committing an offense, it is an unafflicted transgression.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva’s compassion toward an evil person is deeper than toward a virtuous person. Regarding those who do not commit the offense: if they are insane;
or if one knows that by not speaking [of their fault] they will be disciplined, as previously described; or if one protects the mind of another; or if one protects the regulations of the Saṃgha.

Loving-kindness bestows happiness; compassion extracts suffering. A virtuous person knows for themselves how to avoid suffering and seek happiness, whereas an evil person possesses only suffering and no happiness.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply arouses loving-kindness and compassion, just as parents, though they love all their children equally, show particular pity for one who is ill.
△ Eighth, the precepts that differ from those of the śrāvakas. This has two meanings. First, regarding the precept of protecting sentient beings:
one must study together; to differ is to commit an offense. Second, regarding the precept of limited skillful means: one should not study together; to study together is to commit an offense.

If a bodhisattva, within the *prātimokṣa* of the Tathāgata, observes the prohibitions established by the *vinaya* for the sake of protecting sentient beings—causing those without faith to have faith and increasing the faith of those who already have it—they should train in the same manner as the *śrāvakas*. (This refers to bodhisattva-bhikṣus;

since they are renunciants, they should indeed follow the rules of renunciation. Why is this? Because *śrāvakas* do not go beyond their own liberation, and even they must not depart from [the precepts].
[The Buddha] protects others by causing those without faith to have faith, and causing those with faith to increase [in it] and train in the precepts (śīla) of the bhikṣus.

How much more so for a bodhisattva, who benefits both self and others? Since this is the supreme ultimate deliverance, how could one not study these bhikṣu precepts? [If one does not,] this would be a case of "the same yet not the same," which constitutes an offense.

Furthermore, among the prohibitive offenses (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya), there are those that involve limited benefit, limited activity, and limited skillful means; the Blessed One established these specifically for the sake of śrāvakas.
Such a person is a bodhisattva. (Although they may be a bhikṣu,) they do not train in these same precepts. Why is this? Śrāvakas seek their own liberation and abandon others;

therefore, they should abide in few gains, few activities, and few skillful means. It is not the case that a bodhisattva, who seeks both their own liberation and the liberation of others, should likewise abide in few gains, few activities, and few skillful means. For the sake of sentient beings, a bodhisattva [should accept gifts] from those who are not relatives.

(1) To seek hundreds or thousands of robes from brahmins and householders constitutes one [offense]. (2) When those householders offer robes of their own accord, one should observe whether the donor is capable of giving;
regardless of the quantity, if they are capable, one should accept them according to what is offered—this constitutes two. (3) As it is with robes, so it is with alms bowls—this constitutes three.
As it is with robes and bowls, so too is it when one personally begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it—this is likewise [four].
This is so. (This constitutes the fourth. For the sake of sentient beings, one should possess and store bedding and seating made of *kōshaya* (silk);

even up to hundreds of thousands [of such items]—this constitutes the fifth. Even up to hundreds of thousands of gold and silver [items], for the sake of sentient beings, one should also accept them—this constitutes the sixth.

Such are the offenses of concealment (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*) for *śrāvakas* who abide in few gains, few activities, and few skillful means; these are not shared trainings for a Bodhisattva (*bhikṣu*). Having already [established this],...

One who abides in the Bodhisattva’s vows of discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) should act for the sake of all sentient beings. If, with a mind of resentment, one abides in few benefits, few activities, and few skillful means, this is called a transgression of many offenses;

it is a transgression arising from affliction (*kliṣṭa*). If, however, one abides in few benefits, few activities, and few skillful means due to indolence and laziness, the transgression arises non-afflictively (*akliṣṭa*).

(This should not be treated as identical [to the former], for there is a difference in the nature of the fault. (Note: The circle symbol [○] indicates the end of a section or a specific point of emphasis.)

*Miǎn* (the initial tone of *qiān*); it is synonymous with *qiàn*. It means resentment. If it were read as an entering tone, it would carry the meaning of "satisfaction" or "contentment," which is not the intended sense here.
*Prātimokṣa*: This is translated as "preserving liberation" (*baohuajietuo*). It is also translated as "individual liberation" (*biebiejietuo*).

This term refers generally to the precepts of the sevenfold assembly of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions. *Vinaya*: This is translated as "extinction" (*mie*). It is also translated as "discipline" (*lü*).
This refers specifically to the Bhikṣu Vinaya-piṭaka. Within the Dharma of the Vinaya, there are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
As for natural offenses, even a person who has not received the precepts commits an offense according to worldly law;
these include killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and so forth. As for prohibited offenses, [these are established] by the Buddha...
To protect laypeople from the reproach of their disciples, [the Buddha] prohibited such actions so that they would not be committed.
If one violates the Buddha’s regulations, one incurs an offense; therefore, these are also called *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibitory offenses).

For this reason, a Bodhisattva Bhikṣu must, like a Śrāvaka Bhikṣu, uphold the precepts by not acting as a matchmaker, not privately constructing large dwellings, and not remaining in difficult circumstances.
One must not build a dwelling in a location that causes obstruction. One must not defile another's household or engage in evil conduct.
One must not keep extra robes without performing the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification). One must not stay overnight separated from one’s three robes.

One must not have a nun wash one’s used robes. One must not seek an increase in the price for robes. One must not seek to purchase robes by combining funds. One must not request robes more than six times.
One may obtain a mixture of wild silkworm cotton to make bedding, but one must not make bedding of pure black wool.
One must not make a new bedding before six years have passed. One must not use a sitting mat without patching it with old material.
One must not carry wool on a long journey. One must not have a *bhikṣuṇī* dye wool. One must not buy or sell precious objects. Not...

One may engage in buying and selling. One must not keep a bowl with the intent of seeking a better one. One must not seek to have fine robes woven. One must not give a robe and then angrily seize it back.
One must not keep digestive medicines for more than seven days. One must not seek to use rain-cloths at improper times.
One must not divert monastic property into one’s own possession. One must not sleep in the same room as a woman.

One must not stay for more than three nights with a person who has not received the full precepts (*upasampadā*). One must not recite the scriptures together with a person who has not received the precepts.
One must not speak of another’s grave offense to outsiders. One must not speak of the Dharma one has realized to outsiders. One must not [sleep] with a woman...
People often preach the Dharma. One must not dig the earth. One must not damage living plants or trees. One must not spread out monastic bedding and fail to put it away.
One must not leave monastic quarters with bedding unremoved. One must not forcibly seize a place for lodging. One must not drag another bhikṣu out of his room.
One must not sit on a bed with detachable legs atop a multi-storied pavilion. One must not...
One must not build a room that exceeds three stories. One must not go personally to instruct a nun. One must not instruct a nun until sunset.
One must not criticize or debate while instructing a nun. One must not make robes for a nun. One must not sit in private with a nun.
One must not travel with a nun by appointment. One must not travel in the same boat as a nun. One must not accept food because it was praised by a nun. One must not [give]...
When traveling with women, one must not accept more than one meal’s worth of alms. One must not eat in succession from different sources. One must not eat apart from the community.
One must not accept more than two bowls of cakes, parched grain, or rice. One must not fail to perform the ritual for declaring food as "leftover" (*kṛta-śeṣa*).
One must not cause others to violate the rules regarding leftover food. One must not eat at improper times. One must not consume food kept overnight. One must not...
One should take food for oneself; one must not seek out choice foods. One must not give food to non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) oneself.
One must not go to another household without having entrusted one's bowl to someone else. One must not sit forcefully in a dining house or sit in a secluded place.

One must not sit alone with a woman. One must not intentionally cause others to lose their food. One must not accept more invitations for medicine than necessary. One must not observe military forces.
Do not enter battle. Do not drink alcohol. Do not play in the water. Do not strike or tickle one another.
Do not fail to accept admonition. Do not cause others to fear. Do not bathe more than once a day. Do not light fires in the open air.
Do not play by hiding others' belongings. Do not wear robes given as pure offerings (śuddhika) without permission. Do not wear robes that have not been dyed with the prescribed colors. Do not...
Therefore: one must not cause distress to others; one must not conceal the gross offenses of others; one must not bestow the bhikṣu precepts upon those who have not yet reached twenty years of age;
one must not initiate disputes; one must not travel as a companion with bandits; and one must not side with those who hold evil views.
One must not harbor a *śrāmaṇera* who has been suspended. One must not reject admonition or evade difficult questions. One must not lightly deride the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
One must not receive the precepts and remain ignorant of them. One must not violate formal legal procedures (*karmavācanā*). One must not fail to give one's consent (*chanda*).
One must not regret having given one's consent. One must not enter the palace gates at will. One must not handle precious objects at will. One must not...
One must not enter a village at an improper time. One must not use a high bed. One must not use a mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton.
One must not make a needle case from bone or ivory. One must not make a garment for covering sores that exceeds the prescribed measure. One must not make a robe equal in size to the Buddha’s robes.
One must not allow a nun to seek food on one's behalf. One must not receive food from a family that has been designated as such.
One must not receive food in a place where one feels threatened. One must not wear robes that are untidy. One must not enter the house of a layperson with one’s robe tucked up over the shoulder.
Furthermore, one must not preach the Dharma to anyone who is holding a staff, a sword, a blade, a parasol, or similar items. Among these two hundred and fifty precepts:
Excluding only the six precepts concerning minor benefits, minor activities, and minor expedients, the remaining two hundred and forty-four precepts are to be studied together.
If one does not study them, one incurs the same offense as a bhikṣu.
This is because such a bodhisattva-bhikṣu cannot be called a bodhisattva-śrāmaṇera, a bodhisattva-upāsaka, or the like. Bodhi...
Just as it is for a bhikṣu, so it is for a bodhisattva bhikṣuṇī; a bodhisattva śikṣamāṇā must likewise study the six dharmas;
and a bodhisattva śrāmaṇera must likewise study the ten precepts. [Regarding] kauseya:
This refers to "insect-cloth," which is precisely silk floss. It is permitted to be kept for the sake of sentient beings, but its personal use is not permitted.
This is clearly and explicitly stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra* likewise contains earnest admonitions; one must be cautious, one must be cautious.

Furthermore, although a bodhisattva bhikṣu is said not to train in these six precepts of limited gain, limited activity, and limited expedient means, they must nevertheless equally perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification). Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"A bodhisattva first regards all their accumulated requisites as impure, and with a pure mind, relinquishes them to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
For example, when a bhikṣu is about to give away robes currently in his possession to his two teachers (upādhyāya and ācārya), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states:
"Although it is permitted to accept and keep [robes], one must necessarily perform a 'pure gift' (*śuddhika-dāna*) to a donor of sincere faith. The *Fuxingji* by Jingxi says:

"Some people say: 'Regarding all that one possesses, if one regards them as not being one's own property and uses them whenever they are beneficial, what is the purpose of performing a 'pure gift'? Now, we ask:"
These [items] are not one's own property; why then would they not suffice for the four seas? If they are beneficial, one should simply use them.

Why instead entrust them to two fields (out of compassion and respect), locking them away in a deep chamber and sealing them in bags and boxes? This is truly harboring the thought of another’s property; to use such items will inevitably incur transgression (the offense of theft).

If one suddenly claims them as one's own property, this still violates the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification). Thus, we know that those who do not perform the *śuddhi* rite deeply contravene the Buddha’s regulations.
Not subsumed within the two vehicles, nor encompassed by the three roots—if one leaves the household life in such a state, is this not a futile loss? The *Jingxun of the Black-Garment Gate* states:
"In the present age, those who lecture and study devote themselves exclusively to profit and fame; they do not feel shame for the five perversities and frequently accumulate the eight impurities.

They merely follow the drifting customs of the world and never contemplate the words of the Sages. How could they know that all the necessities used daily are nothing but impure things, filling their chests and bags?"

All that has been accumulated consists of wealth acquired through transgressions, born of arrogance toward the Dharma and deceitful intent; one brings this calamity upon oneself. Who knows that retribution follows the mind and is formed?
How could one believe that the fruit is produced by the connection of causes? One sees now that the *kāṣāya* robe leaves the body, yet in the future, iron leaves will wrap around the body.
How much more so for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, which are collectively termed "pure dharmas. If one harbors deep faith, how could one begrudge their practice?
△ Ninth: The Precept Against Erroneous Livelihood.
If a bodhisattva is deceitful and crooked in body or speech—whether by manifesting signs, disparaging others, or seeking gain through such means—they abide in an erroneous livelihood.
Regarding the factor of life and the mind of shamelessness and lack of dread: if one is unable to abandon them, this is called committing many offenses.

This offense arises from defilement. One who does not commit [this offense] is one who, for the sake of severing those [defilements], has applied the desire for skillful means; yet, due to the predominance of afflictions, they arise again and again.
Deceitfulness of body and speech generally clarifies the characteristics of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). As for "manifesting signs":
whether manifesting extraordinary or marvelous signs, or manifesting signs such as coldness or heat, all are deceitfulness of the body. As for "reviling":

whether practicing divination of good and bad fortune and preaching the Dharma to others, or raising one's voice to display authority so as to inspire awe and respect in others, all are [deceitfulness] of speech.

This refers to crookedness and flattery. If one seeks profit through profit—whether by speaking of one's own merits or by describing the offerings one has received to stir the hearts of others—that is also crookedness of speech.
Or, if one gives gifts to laypeople or engages in buying, selling, and lending to seek profit, that too is crookedness of speech. Therefore, it is summarized as "dwelling in wrong livelihood."

This is the Dharma. Because one does not know to respect one’s own numinous spirit, there is no sense of shame (*hrī*); because one does not know to look up to and aspire toward the sages and philosophers, there is no sense of remorse (*apatrāpya*).
Yet, it is said merely that one is defiled and transgresses, rather than saying that one loses the Bodhisattva precepts;
this is simply because the wisdom and vows for Bodhi have not yet been forgotten. Should one fail to repent and reform, one will inevitably bring about defiled fruits.
△ Tenth: The Precept Against Frivolity.

If a bodhisattva is restless and does not delight in tranquility, making loud noises and playing for amusement so as to cause others to find pleasure, by reason of such causes and conditions, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This is a transgression arising from defilement. If it occurs through forgetfulness or error, it is a transgression not arising from defilement.
Regarding the non-offense of engaging [in such actions]: it is for the purpose of severing those [faults], engaging with the desire and skillful means as previously described.

Furthermore, there is no offense if another has given rise to resentment and one acts to cause it to cease; or if another is distressed and one acts to cause that distress to subside; or if another is by nature fond of play.

In order to gather them in, to sever those [faults], and for their protection; and because others might suspect that the bodhisattva harbors resentment or acts in opposition, he displays a cheerful countenance and playful laughter to manifest the purity of his mind.
△ Eleventh: The Perverted Teaching on the Bodhisattva Precepts.
If a bodhisattva holds such a view and speaks thus: "A bodhisattva should not delight in nirvāṇa; they should turn their back upon nirvāṇa.
They should not fear the afflictions (*kleśa*); they should not feel exclusive revulsion toward them. Why is this? A bodhisattva should..."
To speak in such a manner as to have long undergone birth and death throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas in pursuit of great bodhi—this is called committing many offenses.
This offense arises from defilement. Why is this? Because śrāvakas deeply delight in nirvāṇa.
The fear and aversion toward afflictions, even by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, do not equal the Bodhisattva’s profound delight in *nirvāṇa*.
The fear and aversion toward afflictions refers to the Śrāvakas, who act solely for their own benefit; the Bodhisattvas are not like this, as they act universally for the sake of all sentient beings.
Their practice of the undefiled mind surpasses that of the Arhats, who, though accomplished in the tainted (*sāsrava*) state, remain free from afflictions.
This refers to the undefiled mind cultivated by Śrāvaka Arhats; it is the accomplishment of the untainted (anāsrava), free from all afflictions, and is not difficult—like a lotus flower in water.

Now, as for the undefiled mind cultivated by Bodhisattvas, because it is universally for the sake of sentient beings, it must necessarily accomplish the tainted (sāsrava) while still remaining free from all [afflictions].

Afflictions are like a lotus flower within fire; this is most difficult indeed. Were it not for a profound delight in nirvana a hundred-thousand-millionfold greater than one's dread and revulsion toward afflictions, how could one traverse the realm of outflows without giving rise to the faults and calamities of affliction?
If one does not dread and revile afflictions, then one will receive the fruits of birth and death with a defiled mind. Not so.
"In time, one will surely lose the way to Great Bodhi. Such inverted teaching is extreme indeed.

Yet, that this is not termed a *pārājika* offense is merely said with reference to the lower and middle grades [of such views]. If one resolutely gives rise to this superior attachment to views, it constitutes the preaching of a counterfeit Dharma and the slandering of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka."
△ Twelfth: The Precept Against Failing to Guard Against Censure and Contempt.

If a bodhisattva does not guard against words of lack of faith, nor guards against censure and defamation, and likewise fails to eliminate them—if there is actually a fault or evil that is not eliminated—this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement. [If] there is none in reality...

Regarding faults and evils that are not eliminated: there is no offense if they arise without defilement; nor is there an offense if it concerns an outsider who slanders, or other wicked persons (who slander out of malice);
or if one who has gone forth to beg for alms and cultivate wholesome causes and conditions is subjected to the derision and defamation of others;
or if the person before whom one speaks is angry or insane and thus utters such derision—(in these cases, failing to eliminate them is called non-offense).

If there are indeed faults and evils, one ought certainly to reform them and eliminate the resulting censure. Even if there are no faults or evils, one should still distance oneself from suspicion and avoid causing doubt.
Only in the case of externalists, wicked people, or those who are enraged and maliciously slanderous should one not insist on forcibly suppressing or extinguishing [the criticism].
△ Thirteenth: The Precept Against Failing to Subdue Sentient Beings.

If a bodhisattva perceives that a sentient being should be benefited through the skillful means of harsh words, yet refrains from doing so out of fear that it will cause them distress and sorrow, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This offense arises from non-afflictive causes. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].
Observe that in the present, such actions yield little benefit and give rise to much distress and vexation.
△ Fourteenth: The Precept Against Retaliating with Anger, Blows, or Abuse.
If a bodhisattva, when insulted, insults in return; when provoked to anger, returns anger; when struck, strikes back; or when reviled, reviles in return—this is [a transgression].
This is called an offense of many transgressions; it is an offense arising from defilement.
△ Fifteenth: The Precept on Improper Confession and Apology.
If a Bodhisattva offends another person, or even if they have not offended but causes another to suspect them, they should immediately confess and apologize with a sense of remorse.
If one feels regret for having been disrespectful and fails to perform a formal confession and apology according to the Dharma, this is called an offense of many transgressions (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

This offense arises from defilement if it is due to indolence or laziness; it arises without defilement otherwise. There is no offense if, by means of a skillful expedient, one intends to subdue the other person;
or if the other person desires to commit an impure act and only afterwards accepts [the apology], such that an apology is not required and there is no fault; or if one knows that the other person...

Human nature is prone to contention and litigation. If one offers an apology or seeks reconciliation, it only increases the other's anger. If one knows that the other person is harmonious and patient, harboring no resentment, yet refrains from apologizing for fear of causing them shame, there is no fault in doing so.
△ The sixteenth precept on not accepting an apology for an offense:

If a bodhisattva, when another person comes to commit an offense against them and repents according to the Dharma, refuses to accept that repentance out of a heart of resentment and with the intent to vex the other, this is called a transgression of the many offenses;
it is a transgression arising from defilement. However, if it is not out of a heart of resentment... [it is not a transgression].

Not accepting an apology constitutes an offense that arises from non-defilement. There is no offense in the following cases: if one employs skillful means to subdue the person as previously described;
or if the person does not repent according to the Dharma and their mind is not impartial, such that one does not accept their apology. This is without fault.

I became angry with another and did not accept their apology; therefore, the preceding text concludes that this constitutes a grave offense. Another committed an offense against me and I did not accept their apology;
therefore, the present text concludes that this constitutes a light offense.
△ Seventeenth: The Precept Against Resentment Toward Others.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of resentment toward others and clings to it without relinquishing it, this is called a transgression of many offenses.

This constitutes an offense arising from defilement. There is no offense if, for the sake of severing that [defilement], one generates the desire and employs the skillful means as previously described.
△ The eighteenth precept: regarding the offense of greedily maintaining a retinue.
If a bodhisattva, out of greed for service and attendance, maintains a retinue, this is called a transgression of many offenses. This...
This constitutes an offense arising from defilement. One who does not commit the offense is one who maintains [disciples] without a mind of greed.
If there is no mind of greed, then one must certainly examine one's own virtue and conduct: whether one is fit to be a teacher;

whether, having taken on a retinue, one can properly protect them through both material wealth and the Dharma; and even if one can protect them, whether one knows that they will truly rely upon oneself.
Does it increase supramundane karma? Even if it slightly benefits that fruit, does it not hinder or damage one's own practice?
If it fails to benefit both oneself and others, it remains merely the pursuit of greed and service. Should one not be cautious?
△ Nineteenth: The Precept Against Indulgence in Sleep.
If a bodhisattva is indolent and lazy, or indulges in the pleasure of sleep, or does so at improper times or without moderation, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This is a transgression arising from defilement. There is no offense if one is ill, lacks physical strength, or is traveling a long distance.
Exhausted. If, for the sake of severing that [exhaustion], one arouses desire and applies skillful means as previously described.

△ Twenty: Regarding the *Lokāyatika-sūtra* and the precept on time—if a bodhisattva, with a defiled mind, discusses worldly treatises (*lokāyata*) at the improper time, this is called a transgression of many [precepts].
This constitutes an offense. If it arises from defilement, it is a defiled offense; if one forgets or errs after some time has passed, it is a non-defiled offense.

There is no offense if, while observing others engaged in conversation, one listens for a brief moment in order to protect their feelings; or if one briefly answers another's question regarding something they have not previously heard.
△ Twenty-first: Not Accepting the Teacher’s Instruction and Admonition.
If a bodhisattva, desiring to seek a concentrated mind, harbors resentment and pride and does not accept the teacher’s instruction, this is called a transgression of many offenses;
it is a transgression arising from defilement. If it is due to indolence or laziness, it is a transgression not arising from defilement. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].
If one is ill, or lacks strength, or knows that the other person is speaking erroneously; or if one is oneself learned and capable,
or has already received the Dharma previously—
one who desires to seek a concentrated mind must necessarily consult and receive the teacher’s instruction, and only then may one practice according to that teaching.
There has never been one who, being reckless and superficial, could suddenly advance in their practice.
Some, suspecting that the teacher’s instructions are overly detailed and not direct or expedient, harbor resentment and arrogance, refusing to accept them;
thus, their transgression is actually heavier than that of the indolent or the forgetful. How can those who study today not be cautious?
△ Twenty-second: The precept regarding the mind following the five hindrances.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to the five hindrances in the mind and does not awaken to them, this is called a transgression of many offenses;
it is a transgression arising from defilement. There is no transgression if, for the sake of severing them, one generates the desire and applies the means as previously described.

The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*) are: first, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; and fifth, doubt. Regarding the hindrance of sensual desire:
when one is correctly practicing meditative concentration and wisdom, the mind intensely contemplates the five sensory objects and cannot be stilled even for a moment.
Regarding the hindrance of ill will: when one is correctly practicing meditative concentration and wisdom, the mind intensely contemplates an enemy.
The hindrance of attachment to home (*gṛha-nīvaraṇa*): one cannot forget it for even a moment. The hindrance of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*):

when correctly practicing meditative concentration and wisdom, the body and mind become heavy and dull, unable to maintain themselves. The hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*):

when correctly practicing meditative concentration and wisdom, the three karmas become scattered and drifting, unable to find peace within themselves. Restlessness itself is not called a hindrance; because restlessness is difficult to restrain, it gives rise to remorse. Remorse...

Like a poisoned arrow, that which can obstruct meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is termed a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*). Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), there are further three types:
first, doubt regarding the Dharma, meaning one thinks that this Dharma may not necessarily enable the attainment of meditative concentration and wisdom;

second, doubt regarding the person, meaning one thinks that although the teacher instructs me in the methods for cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom, since he himself has not yet realized various forms of such concentration and wisdom, why should I rely upon him? Third, doubt...
One may say to oneself: "My faculties are dull and my hindrances are deep; how could I possibly cultivate and realize the various forms of dhyāna and wisdom?
Any one of these five hindrances of the mind, as soon as it arises, becomes a great obstacle. One must urgently employ skillful means to awaken from them.

When the hindrance of sensual desire arises, one should contemplate impurity, impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. When the hindrance of ill-will arises, one should reflect that there is truly no self or person.
When the hindrance of sloth and torpor arises, one should exert effort and remain vigilant through walking meditation.
When the hindrance of restlessness and remorse arises, one should bind the mind to a single point and gradually subdue it, rather than indulging in regret.

When the hindrance of doubt arises, one should recollect the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which is certainly free from falsehood; for although the teacher may be an ordinary person, they are able to expound the noble Dharma, just as a mother provides nourishment.

Do not disdain the milk because of its foul appearance; do not disdain the crookedness of a branch when gathering fruit from a tree. One's latent potential (*gotra*) is difficult to fathom, so one must not abandon oneself.
Since obstacles have no inherent nature, one should not disparage oneself.
△ Twenty-third: Taking Worldly Dhyāna as a Precept.
If a bodhisattva perceives the savoring of dhyāna (*āsvādana-dhyāna*) as a spiritual merit, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This is a transgression arising from defilement. There is no offense if, for the sake of abandoning that [savoring], one generates the desire and applies the skillful means as previously described.

When non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings cultivate the contemplation of the six practices—disgust for the lower realms as suffering, coarseness, and obstruction, and aspiration for the higher realms as purity, subtlety, and liberation—the four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments they achieve are termed "tasting dhyāna" (*āsvādita-dhyāna*).

This is because their realization is obscure and lacks the wisdom derived from hearing; consequently, they give rise to craving and attachment at each stage, and their meditative objects remain indistinct.
If, however, a disciple of the Buddha cultivates according to the Six Sublime Gates, the Sixteen Special Victories, and so forth...
This is merely a means to counteract the distraction of desire and to give rise to supramundane right wisdom; it is not that this [meditative state] itself constitutes a true spiritual merit.
If one were to suddenly attain a meditative state and become attached to its flavor, how would this differ from ordinary worldlings?
One would inevitably be reborn according to the level of that meditation and fall away from the path to Great Enlightenment. Is this not perilous?
△ Twenty-fourth: The Precept Against Slandering the Śrāvaka Dharma.
If a bodhisattva holds such a view and speaks thus, saying: "A bodhisattva should not listen to the sūtras and teachings of the śrāvakas;
they should not accept them, nor should they study them. Of what use are the śrāvaka teachings to a bodhisattva? This is called committing a transgression of the many offenses.
This constitutes an offense arising from defilement. Why? Because a bodhisattva would even listen to the heterodox arguments of outsiders, let alone the words of the Buddha.
It is not an offense if one is exclusively studying the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and has not yet been able to master it completely.
△ Twenty-fifth: The Transgression of Turning Away from the Great and Toward the Small.

If a bodhisattva, regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, fails to apply skillful means and abandons it without studying it, instead exclusively practicing the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas, this is called a transgression of many offenses. This transgression arises from non-affliction.

Regarding the former precept, to disparage the Śrāvaka teachings results in the loss of both the Great and the Small Vehicles; therefore, its transgression constitutes a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*).
Regarding this precept, to abandon the Great Vehicle and practice only the Small Vehicle makes the Small the very foundation for the Great; therefore, its transgression is not a defiled offense.

By observing these two precepts, it is clear that those in future generations who pride themselves on being Mahāyāna followers while being dissatisfied with the minor details of the Small Vehicle deeply violate the instructions of the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya).
△ Twenty-sixth: Not Training in the Buddha’s Precepts.

If a bodhisattva, regarding what has been taught by the Buddha, abandons it and does not train in it, but instead practices the heterodox treatises of external paths or worldly scriptures, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This is a transgression arising from defilement. There is no offense if one is of superior intelligence.

One is able to quickly receive and study the Buddha’s scriptures; if one has studied them for a long time, one does not forget them; if one has contemplated the scriptures, one deeply understands their meaning.
Regarding the Buddha’s teachings, one has already performed thorough investigation and is now able to attain unshakable wisdom (which can never be moved by external doctrines).
Furthermore, on a daily basis, one should spend two parts of the superior time studying the Buddha’s scriptures, and one part of the inferior time engaging with external texts.
This is called non-offense. Thus, a bodhisattva who avoids even a single inferior moment of engaging with external treatises, yet remains proficient in worldly scriptures and those of non-Buddhists—

To take pleasure in and fail to abandon heterodox doctrines (which follow the views of worldly scholars), and not to regard them as poison (failing to recognize the faults and afflictions of both craving and views)—this is called committing many offenses.
This offense arises from defilement.
The Vinaya states: "In order to subdue outsiders, it is permitted to read non-Buddhist texts once during each of the three periods of the day;
however, one must not adopt the views arising from those texts. For one who wishes to subdue others, it is inappropriate to cherish or delight in them.
Knowing that they cannot lead to liberation from birth and death, one should regard them as poison."
△ Twenty-seventh: The Precept Against Disbelief in Profound Dharmas.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the profound meaning of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, its true meaning, or the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, slanders them and refuses to accept them, saying, "These are not beneficial;
they were not spoken by the Tathāgata," then this person is likewise unable to abide in peace and happiness.

Sentient beings—this is called committing numerous offenses. This offense arises from defilement, either because of one's own improper mental reflection leading to slander, or because of following others in slandering;
in all such cases, an offense is committed. When this Bodhisattva hears the foremost, most profound meaning...

Even if one cannot immediately give rise to a mind of understanding, this bodhisattva should nevertheless exert themselves to develop faith in this profound meaning, rather than a crooked or deceitful mind.

With such a mind, they should train as follows, reproaching themselves: "I was originally not so; I am blind, lacking the eye of wisdom. The Tathāgata, however, possesses the ten powers and the eye of wisdom.
Thus, he speaks this teaching of the ultimate truth in accordance with those of superior faculties. Furthermore, the Tathāgata also has other teachings [to accommodate others].

We are persons of shallow capacity; yet whether deep or shallow, all these are the Buddha’s teachings, all being the Dharma corresponding to the capacities of beings through the Buddha’s eye of wisdom. How could we now give rise to slander out of our own delusion?

If a Bodhisattva can thus recognize their own place of retreat, and regarding such dharmas as the Tathāgata presently knows and sees, they contemplate them with right mindfulness and incline toward them with right faith—this is called not committing an offense. It is because it is not due to a lack of understanding that they give rise to slander; therefore, there is no offense.
The meaning of profundity refers to both phenomena and principle transcending emotional cognition and departing from dualistic views.

The meaning of reality is that phenomena in their entirety are identical to the principle of the Dharma-realm; the three truths are perfectly interfused and inconceivable, as it is said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi."
This refers to such statements as "birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa" and so forth. Regarding the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:
they fully manifest wondrous events through the principle, containing and encompassing one another in infinite layers that can never be exhausted.
As it is said: "Within the tip of a single hair, the jeweled king of lands appears; sitting within a mote of dust, they turn the Great Dharma Wheel," and so forth. To state the essential point:

Within the Great Canon of the Teachings, there are many matters and principles that surpass ordinary thought. Although one may not immediately understand them, one should still believe in them with reverence;
one must never hastily give rise to slander. I entrust this to future sages: you should be especially careful regarding this matter.
△ Twenty-eighth: Praising Oneself and Slandering Others Regarding Precepts.
If a bodhisattva, with a mind of greed or anger, praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is called a transgression of many offenses;
it is an offense arising from defilement. There is no offense if one disparages non-Buddhists in order to extol the Buddha-dharma. If...

One employs skillful means to subdue them as previously described. Furthermore, regarding "not committing an offense": it means causing those without faith to gain faith, and causing those with faith to increase and expand it.
As for "praising one's own virtues," although one may possess actual virtues, one praises them out of a greedy mind. "Slandering others" [is likewise forbidden].
Although there may be actual faults [in the person], one slanders them with a mind of anger. Because of greed one praises; because of anger one slanders.

Since these two states of mind certainly do not arise simultaneously, each is separately classified as a light offense (*āpatti*). If, however, one uses a mind of greed to compare oneself with others, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
Only when comparing the Buddha-dharma with non-Buddhist paths is it for the purpose of "crushing the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox"; therefore, no offense is committed.
Regarding the precepts: furthermore, if one employs skillful means to subdue sentient beings, causing them to abandon their evils and learn one's own virtues, there is likewise no transgression.
Moreover, if through praise or censure one can cause those without faith to believe and those who already believe to increase in their faith, there is also no violation of the precepts.
This must be based on a true understanding of the individual's capacity; it cannot be indiscriminately cited as a precedent.
△ Twenty-ninth: The Precept Against Refusing to Listen to the Dharma Out of Arrogance.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing of a place where the Dharma is being taught or a place for definitive discussion, does not go to listen due to a mind of arrogance or a mind of resentment, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement. [However,] if it is due to laziness or indolence...

The offense arises from non-defiled motivation. There is no offense if one does not understand; or if one is ill; or if one lacks strength; or if the other person teaches the Dharma erroneously; or if one protects the mind of the speaker;

or if one has heard it repeatedly, already mastered it, and understood its meaning; or if one is widely learned or possesses the faculty of retaining what is heard; or if one practices according to the teaching;
or if one is practicing meditative concentration and does not wish to interrupt it even for a moment; or if one is of dull faculties and finds it difficult to realize.
It is difficult to receive and difficult to uphold. For those who do not go [to hear the teaching], there is no offense.
△ The thirtieth precept: Regarding the Precept Against Despising Dharma Teachers.
If a bodhisattva treats a Dharma teacher with contempt, fails to give rise to reverence, mocks and reviles them, and clings only to the literal words of the text, it is an offense.
According to the true meaning, this is called committing many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
Among those who preach the Dharma, some possess both excellent phrasing and excellent meaning, while others possess excellent meaning but coarse phrasing.
There are instances where the phrasing is elegant while the meaning is shallow; therefore, those who listen to the Dharma should rely solely on the meaning and not on the phrasing.
Should one, because the phrasing appears crude, give rise to derision or disparagement, the fault is profound indeed.
△ Thirty-first: The Precept of Not Engaging in Different Activities. A bodhisattva has four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) by which they gather in sentient beings:
first, giving; second, kind speech; third, beneficial conduct; and fourth, common purpose. This present case refers to gathering them through common purpose.
If a bodhisattva, abiding in the morality of restraint, sees sentient beings engaged in various activities and, out of a mind of resentment, does not engage in joint labor with them—
namely, in deliberating on various matters, whether traveling on a journey, engaging in lawful enterprise for profit, managing agricultural estates, or tending cattle.
If one does not participate in the reconciliation of disputes, in auspicious assemblies, or in meritorious deeds, this is called a "multitudinous offense" (prāyaścittika).
This offense arises from defilement if it is due to indolence or laziness; it does not arise from defilement if it is due to such factors. There is no offense if one is ill.

If one lacks the power; if the other person is capable of accomplishing it themselves; if the other person already has many companions; if the task to be performed is contrary to the Dharma or not conducive to the ultimate goal;
if one can subdue them through skillful means as previously described; if one has already made a prior commitment to another; if the other person harbors enmity toward oneself;
if one is personally cultivating wholesome karma and does not wish to interrupt it even for a moment; if one is by nature dull-witted; or if one is protecting the feelings of many people.
If one protects the monastic regulations and does not act in concert with others, there is no offense in any of these cases.
Regarding matters such as developing profitable agricultural estates and raising cattle, these are exclusively for the lay bodhisattva to engage in.
If one engages in traveling, reconciling disputes, auspicious gatherings, meritorious deeds, and so forth, then these should likewise apply to the renunciant bodhisattva.
There are twelve types of non-offenses; each begins with the character "yi" (若), as can be understood.
△ The Thirty-second Precept: Not Tending to the Sick (which here also clarifies not tending to the poor and suffering).
If a Bodhisattva, seeing a person who is weak and ill, does not go to visit them out of a mind of anger and resentment, this is called a transgression of many offenses;
it is a transgression arising from defilement. If it is due to laziness or indolence, it is a transgression not arising from defilement. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].
If one is ill oneself; or if one lacks strength; or if one instructs someone who has strength to attend to the sick person;
