or if one knows that the person has their own relatives; or if that person has the strength to manage the situation themselves; or if the illness recurs frequently; or if it is a chronic illness;

or if one is cultivating superior practices and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment; or if one is dull-witted, making it difficult to awaken, difficult to receive [the teaching], difficult to maintain, and difficult to abide in the object of focus. Or...
First, observe his illness. Whether he has committed an offense or not, and whether he is in a state of poverty and suffering or not, it is the same.
"Abiding amidst adverse conditions. The Tang translation says: "Difficult [to practice], one abides by focusing the mind upon those conditions.

This means that for a person of dull faculties, even though they bind the mind to a single object, it is difficult for the mind to remain fixed on a single focal point. The rest may be understood accordingly.
△ The thirty-third precept: Not Admonishing Evil Persons.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings committing unwholesome deeds in this life and future lives, yet out of a heart of resentment does not provide them with correct instruction, this is called a transgression of many offenses.
This is a transgression arising from defilement. There is no offense if one lacks personal wisdom.
If one lacks the power; or if one causes another who possesses power to speak; or if that person already possesses power themselves; or if that person already has virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
or if one employs skillful means (*upāya*) to subdue them as previously described; or if one speaks correctly but they harbor hatred toward me;

or if one speaks correctly but they necessarily utter harsh words; or if one speaks correctly but they necessarily distort it; or if they have no affection or respect for me at all and will certainly not accept what is said.

Furthermore, if that person is of a base and perverse nature (such that one cannot converse with them—*lóng*: pronounced *lì dǒng* in the level tone, meaning unregulated; also in the even tone, meaning full of evil; or in the departing tone, meaning a hateful disposition).

That which can bring about retribution in the present life is called "evil karma of this life. That which can bring about retribution in future lives or subsequent rebirths is called "evil karma of future lives.
Furthermore, acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are called "evil karma of this life.
To seek the five desires and long life among humans or in the heavens while practicing generosity, morality, and meditation is called "evil karma of future lives. The former...
Regarding the former evil karma, because of delusion concerning the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), one should correctly explain the causes and effects of the mundane world.
Regarding the latter evil karma, because of delusion concerning the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), one should correctly explain the causes and effects of the supramundane.
△ The thirty-fourth precept on failing to repay kindness:

If a bodhisattva receives a favor from another yet, out of resentment, does not offer a response—meaning they do not repay that person with an equivalent or greater benefit—it is called a transgression of many offenses.
This is an offense arising from defilement. [It is also an offense] if one is indolent or lazy.
Negligence. An offense arises from non-afflicted motivation. There is no offense if one employs a means but lacks the power;
or if one employs a means to subdue the other as previously described; or if one wishes to repay a kindness, but the other person does not accept it.
△ Thirty-fifth Precept: Not Consoling Those in Grief and Distress.

If a bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings facing hardships regarding their relatives or their wealth, fails—out of resentment—to provide consolation and remove their grief and distress, this is called a transgression of many offenses. This offense arises from defilement. [If it is due to] laziness...
Laziness and indolence. This constitutes an offense arising from non-defiled negligence. There is no offense in cases as previously explained regarding different matters.
△ The thirty-sixth precept: Not giving material wealth.
If a bodhisattva, when requested for food, drink, or clothing, fails to provide them due to a mind of anger and resentment, this is called an offense.
This constitutes a transgression of many offenses. If it arises from defilement, it is an offense of defiled origin; if it arises from indolence or laziness, it is an offense of non-defiled origin.
There is no offense if one lacks the object oneself, or if one seeks an object that is not in accordance with the Dharma, or if the object would not benefit the other person.

Furthermore, there is no offense if one employs skillful means to subdue the other as previously described, or if the other person has violated the laws of the king and one acts to protect the king's mind, or to uphold the regulations of the Saṃgha.

Although one does not give alms, one also refrains from disparaging [the recipient]; therefore, only a light offense is incurred. Furthermore, it may be that the stinginess is of middling or inferior grade rather than superior;
thus, a light offense is incurred. There are six types of non-offenses, all of which may be understood accordingly.
△ The thirty-seventh precept on the improper gathering of disciples:
If a bodhisattva gathers a following and, out of a mind of resentment, fails to provide them with instruction in accordance with the Dharma;
or if he is unable to seek at appropriate times from brahmins and householders clothing, food, bedding, medicine, and dwellings to provide for them as required.
This is called an offense of many transgressions. It is an offense arising from defilement if committed through laziness, indolence, or negligence;
it is an offense not arising from defilement if committed otherwise. There is no offense if one employs skillful means to subdue the person as previously described;

or if protecting the regulations of the Saṃgha; or if one is ill; or if one lacks the strength; or if one causes someone who has the strength to speak; or if the other person is powerful and has many acquaintances.
Venerable One, one who seeks the requisites for oneself, or who has already received instruction and personally knows the Dharma, or an outsider who has stolen the Dharma and cannot be tamed—
such a person may, if they delight in the practice of solitude, choose not to gather a following. However, if they do accept a following, they must necessarily...

One should protect [the Dharma] by means of two things: namely, the Dharma and material wealth. As for the Dharma, it consists of teaching according to the Dharma the trainings in morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
As for material wealth, it consists of providing the four requisites, such as food and clothing. Whether an act constitutes an offense or not may be understood from the text as it stands.
Regarding the phrase "non-Buddhists who steal the Dharma": these were originally non-Buddhists who falsely assumed the guise of disciples, their intention being to plunder [the teachings].
One who takes up the True Dharma to attach it to a heterodox school— having previously failed to perceive their state of mind or divine vision and thus mistakenly accepted them,
yet now being unable to bring them under discipline— does not incur an offense by neither protecting them with material goods nor the Dharma.
△ The thirty-eighth is the precept of not following others. This corresponds to the third of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
Among the ten great king-like vows of Samantabhadra, it is called "constantly acceding to sentient beings.
One should know that when sentient beings have tasks, one goes to assist them; this is called "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*). When sentient beings seek their aspirations, I should...
To grant permission is called "following others.
If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of resentment, does not follow others, this is called a transgression of many offenses;
it is a transgression arising from defilement. If it is due to laziness or indolence, the transgression arises without defilement. There is no transgression if [the other person] intends to...
It is not contrary to the Dharma if one acts thus when ill, when lacking strength, when observing the regulations of the Saṃgha, when that person’s actions— though otherwise lawful—
would cause many others to engage in unlawful matters, when it is for the sake of subduing non-Buddhists, or when it is by means of skillful means to bring them under discipline.
△ Thirty-ninth: The Precept Against Not Rejoicing in Merit.
If a bodhisattva, knowing that other sentient beings possess genuine merit, out of a heart of resentment neither speaks of it to others nor praises it;
and if there is someone who praises it, they do not exclaim "Excellent!"—this is called a transgression of many offenses. This constitutes a violation.
It arises from defilement. If it is due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, it is a non-defiled offense.

There is no offense if one knows that the other person has few desires and acts thus to protect their mind; or if one is ill; or if one lacks the strength; or if one employs skillful means to subdue them;
or if it is to uphold the regulations of the Saṃgha; or if it would cause that person to give rise to afflictions, excessive joy, pride, or what is unbeneficial—excluding these cases.

Because of various faults [one does not speak or praise; there is no offense]. If it is a genuine merit that appears as if it were not a merit, or if it is a genuine eloquent teaching that appears as if it were not an eloquent teaching, [one does not speak or praise;
there is no offense]. If it is for the purpose of subduing the false views of non-Buddhists, [one does not speak or praise; there is no offense].
If one waits until the teaching is finished before then praising it and declaring it excellent, [there is no offense].
Regarding the two phrases "if it is a real merit" and so forth, according to other translations, they should be correctly rendered as: "If it resembles a merit but is not actually a merit;
if it resembles a well-spoken teaching but is not actually a well-spoken teaching. Only then would both the words and the logic be consistent.

At present, this is because the translator did not fully render the phrasing; however, I dare not alter the text. By merely adding explanatory characters, the intended meaning will become clear of itself.
△ Forty: The Precept Against Failing to Subdue with Dignity.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who ought to be rebuked, those who ought to be subdued, or those who ought to be punished and expelled, yet fails to rebuke them due to a defiled mind; or rebukes them but does not subdue them; or subdues them but...
Not to punish or expel [the offender] is called a transgression of many offenses. This transgression arises from defilement.
If the offense is due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, it does not arise from defilement. There are cases where there is no offense:

when the person is incurable, cannot be spoken with, is difficult to instruct, and frequently gives rise to resentment (and is therefore left unpunished, unrebuked, and unexpelled—this being what is known as the method of silent ostracism). If one observes the proper timing (and subsequently rebukes and subdues them...)

[or] expulsion. [However, one does not censure, subdue, or expel him] if one fears that it would cause strife, contention, opposition, or mutual litigation; or if it would lead to a dispute within the Saṃgha or the schism of the Saṃgha;
or if he is not deceitful and possesses a sense of shame and remorse, such that he will gradually reform and repent of himself (and thus requires no censure or the like).
There are three grades of offenses. Minor ones should be subject to censure; middling ones should be subject to subjugation; and major ones should be subject to punishment and expulsion.

Furthermore, an offense committed through negligence may be excused, whereas an offense committed intentionally should be censured. If one does not reform after being censured, they should be subjected to subjugation.

If one does not reform after being subjected to subjugation, they should be punished and expelled. However, if the relationship with their kinsmen is particularly close, or if they have received benefits from them, [these measures must be applied with consideration].
To nurture them while temporarily excusing [their faults] is both termed a "defiled mind" and constitutes the arising of a transgression of defilement.
△ Forty-first: The Precept of Not Using Supernatural Powers for Coercion or Discipline.
If a bodhisattva has already accomplished various supernatural powers, they should then terrify those who ought to be terrified, and... [should discipline those who ought to be disciplined].

One who is to be guided should be guided. Because one wishes to cause sentient beings to consume their offerings of faith, if one does not employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to guide them by means of intimidation, this is called a transgression of many offenses. This transgression arises from non-afflictive origins.

There is no transgression if one knows that those sentient beings would, upon seeing such supernatural powers, give rise to further defiled attachment; or if it would cause non-Buddhists to slander the Noble Ones; or if it would conversely lead to [their] success [in their own views].

Because he holds wrong views, one does not lead him [to the truth] by means of causing fear; thus, there is no offense. Furthermore, if he were to go mad upon seeing such supernormal power (ṛddhi), or if his painful sensations were to increase due to that supernormal power, one does not lead him by means of causing fear; thus, there is no offense.

Even Bodhisattvas who have already perfected their supernormal powers (ṛddhi) still commit transgressions; therefore, the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) cannot be brought to ultimate fulfillment except at the stage of Buddhahood.
This concludes the second section, the detailed enumeration.
○ Third, the inquiry by questioning:
"O Great Beings, many *duṣkṛta* dharmas have already been explained. If a Bodhisattva violates any one of these dharmas, he should perform the *duṣkṛta* confession.
If he does not confess, it will obstruct the Bodhisattva precepts. Now I ask the Great Beings: regarding these matters, are you pure?"
"Pure, pure" (recited three times). "The Great Beings are pure herein, for they remain silent. This matter is thus maintained.
Among these many dharmas, if one violates even a single dharma, one should immediately repent.
If one does not repent, although the precepts are not lost, they will obstruct the precepts—just as dust obscures a mirror or clouds obscure the sun, such that they cannot manifest clearly.
This is the path of the Bodhisattva. Do not treat minor offenses lightly, thinking they will bring no calamity. Although a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
If one repeatedly commits transgressions without generating a sense of weary detachment, the accumulation of light faults will become heavy, and one may even lose their precepts.
This is as clearly explained in the *Karmavācanā* texts; how can one not be cautious? Second, the formal listing of the characteristics of the precepts is concluded.

III. Concluding Summary of the Essential Tenets (in three parts): First, a concluding summary pointing to the functional efficacy of the precepts; second, an exhortation showing the essential core of the mind for upholding them;
third, a concluding summary revealing the benefits of guarding the precepts. Now, the first part.
"O Great Beings, I have already explained the four *pārājika* dharmas of a bodhisattva and the numerous *duṣkṛta* dharmas.

These are the *mātṛkā* of the World-Honored One Maitreya, spoken in unison. This very *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint) is the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering virtuous qualities), and it is the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of benefiting sentient beings).
These various rules of morality can give rise to the bodhisattva practice and can bring the bodhisattva path to fulfillment."

When one initiates practice, the myriad virtues are adorned; this is the power of the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*yuan-yin*). When one attains the Way, the single nature reaches its ultimate perfection;
this is the power of the Buddha-nature as the cognitive cause (*liao-yin*). Both proceed from this precept. How great indeed is the efficacy of the precept!
II. Exhortation to Guard the Essential Heart-Precept:
"O Great Beings, those who wish to resolve their minds to seek Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should skillfully guard and uphold [this precept].
If they so guard and uphold it, they will not give rise to thoughts that this is the Age of Semblance Dharma or that the Dharma is coming to an end."
It is only by generating the great bodhicitta that one obtains the pure precepts of a bodhisattva; it is only by guarding the pure precepts of a bodhisattva that one accomplishes unsurpassed bodhi.

These are mutually dependent, and one cannot be separated from the other for even a moment. That this is so during the Semblance Dharma and Final Dharma periods is merely the deluded perception and discrimination of sentient beings.
Since one wishes to guard and uphold the sublime precepts of a bodhisattva, one must necessarily [cultivate] deeply...
Contemplate that the nature of dharmas is eternally abiding; it is no different from when the Buddha was in the world.

That is to say, the single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa remains solemnly without dispersing. How can you give rise to the thought that the Semblance Dharma has begun and the True Dharma is extinguished, merely seeking to excuse yourself?
Third, the three points clarify the benefits of guarding the precepts:
they can cause the true meaning of the Semblance Dharma to blaze forth; they can ensure that the True Dharma never perishes; and they enable the mind to attain stability.

One will spontaneously accomplish the Buddha-dharma, transform sentient beings, and remain forever free from weariness. With virtuous karma brought to completion, one will swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
It is said that if one upholds these precepts, then even in an age of Semblance Dharma, the true meaning shall continue to blaze forth.
It is just as if the True Dharma were to abide in the world without change; it can cause the Tathāgata’s True Dharma to abide eternally in the world, never to perish.
Because one constantly dwells securely in the True Dharma, the mind attains stillness and abides; one is thus able to personally accomplish the Buddha-dharma—this is the ultimate benefit for oneself.
To then use this very [realization] to teach and transform sentient beings constitutes skillful means.
Thus, one is always free from weariness and fatigue; this is the ultimate benefit for others. When the mind attains stability, this is the power of the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint).

To spontaneously fulfill the Buddha-dharma is the power of the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas). To teach and transform sentient beings while remaining forever free from weariness and fatigue is the power of the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of benefiting sentient beings).
Through these three clusters of morality (*tri-śīla*), one brings about the two benefits; therefore, there is no [exhaustion] in wholesome karma.
It is not ultimately firm; why doubt that one will swiftly attain the Buddha-way? Profound indeed is the great benefit of guarding the precepts.
*Pusa jieben jing jianyao* (Essential Annotations on the Bodhisattva Precept Text), completed.
